svg.aria-label: Azure forced tunnelling: the two VPN gateway configuration methods, the Azure Firewall management interface requirement, the SNAT inversion that hides source addresses, what stops working, and the gateway subnet that must be exempted
svg.title: Forced tunnelling sends everything outbound to on-premises for inspection, and its default SNAT behaviour hides from that perimeter the source address it was deployed to see
svg.text: One sentence of intent, three mechanisms — and a default that argues with the purpose
TWO WAYS TO TURN IT ON, ON A VPN GATEWAY
Via BGP
advertise a default route of 0.0.0.0/0 from on-premises, so all Azure traffic
is sent via the site-to-site tunnel.
Via Default Site
assign ONE local network gateway, in PowerShell — the portal CANNOT do it.
The on-prem VPN device must use 0.0.0.0/0 as its traffic selectors.
A route-based gateway is required. In the worked example there are FOUR cross-premises connections and only one is the Default Site, so the
estate gets a single designated exit — one inspection point, and one dependency for every subnet not exempted.
THE AZURE FIREWALL VARIANT NEEDS A PUBLIC IP TO AVOID PUBLIC IPs
You must create the firewall with the Firewall MANAGEMENT network interface enabled.
That interface carries a public IP used EXCLUSIVELY by the Azure platform, which cannot be
used for any other purpose. The data path can have none.
So “nothing here has a public IP” cannot be met literally. One address remains, carrying platform management rather than workload traffic.
THE SNAT INVERSION — THE DEFAULT DEFEATS THE PURPOSE
Azure Firewall SNATs all outbound traffic to PUBLIC destinations, and does not SNAT to RFC 1918
private ranges. That logic “works perfectly when you egress directly to the Internet.”
But the destination is STILL public under forced tunnelling. So the SNAT fires, and your on-premises
firewall sees every flow from a firewall private address. Per-source rules and logs lose their answer.
The fix, and its price:
add 0.0.0.0/0 as the private IP range and the firewall never SNATs —
and then it can NEVER egress directly to the Internet. No fallback, by configuration.
Narrower option: name only your public-but-internal ranges, keeping attribution without closing the direct exit.
WHAT STOPS WORKING
Azure service traffic
normally stays on the Microsoft backbone regardless of region. Overriding
0.0.0.0/0 sends it down the tunnel instead — blob, Key Vault, queues.
A service endpoint escapes it, because its prefixes are LONGER than 0.0.0.0/0.
KMS activation
the documented casualty. Needs an explicit split-tunnel route on
AzureFirewallSubnet. Fails quietly and late.
Inbound from internet
the subnet is no longer directly reachable. DNAT is documented as NOT
supported with forced tunnelling — and, in the next sentence, as supported
on firewalls with a Management NIC. The docs do not reconcile these. Test it.
The None drop routes
adding the default route REMOVES them, so traffic to unclaimed private
ranges is now forwarded on-premises instead of dropped at the subnet.
Unlike the internet, your on-prem network may well have routes to RFC 1918 space.
EXEMPTIONS — AND THE SUBNET THAT MUST NEVER BE INCLUDED
Exempt a subnet with a route table: a route named ToInternet, 0.0.0.0/0, next hop INTERNET. Applied per
subnet, and it works whether forced tunnelling came from a Default Site or from BGP.
GatewaySubnet must NEVER get a 0.0.0.0/0 route, and route propagation must NEVER be disabled on
it. Either stops the gateway functioning — the gateway this whole policy routes through.
So “apply a default route to every subnet” is both a one-line statement of the requirement and an outage.
The exception belongs in the policy as code, not in someone’s memory at apply time.
With Azure Firewall the egress path is a route on AzureFirewallSubnet rather than a gateway setting, so the platform team owns the change. Propagate
gateway routes is deliberately enabled there — the same property that drops static routes as well as BGP ones when switched off.
In Virtual WAN, forced tunnel is available only on a secured hub that uses routing intent, so managed-hub parity is not automatic.
Before enabling: enumerate the platform’s own outbound dependencies — activation, updates, agent telemetry, time. Each needs a path or a split-tunnel route.
